content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published guidelines and standard operating procedures (SOPs) for the enhanced reporting of acute viral hepatitis cases. These guidelines are part of the WHO's broader strategy to eliminate viral hepatitis as a public health threat. The document outlines technical approaches for acute hepatitis surveillance, emphasizing the importance of differentiating between acute and chronic hepatitis infections and identifying risk factors for new infections. Under the terms of the WHO license, the content can be copied, redistributed, and adapted for non-commercial purposes, provided proper citation is given. The guidelines highlight the need for surveillance systems to monitor acute hepatitis cases, which provide critical information on new infections. Surveillance should focus on acute hepatitis to estimate incidence rates and identify risk factors for transmission. Acute hepatitis surveillance differs from chronic hepatitis reporting, which is typically managed through patient registries. WHO recommends using standardized case definitions that combine clinical symptoms and biomarker criteria to improve specificity and exclude chronic infections. Two key surveillance activities are described: syndromic surveillance and enhanced case reporting. Syndromic surveillance involves reporting clinical cases of acute hepatitis without laboratory confirmation and is useful for detecting outbreaks, particularly of hepatitis A and E. Enhanced case reporting, on the other hand, involves detailed data collection, including laboratory testing and risk factor analysis, to identify trends and transmission routes. This approach is resource-intensive and often limited to high-income countries or sentinel sites in lowand middle-income countries. The SOPs provide criteria for selecting sentinel sites for enhanced case reporting. These sites must have the capacity for in-vitro diagnostic testing, access to patients with acute hepatitis, and sufficient human resources to conduct interviews and collect data. Sentinel sites should prioritize healthcare facilities where most acute hepatitis cases are likely to present, such as outpatient clinics, emergency departments, and hospitals. The document also outlines procedures for data collection, including the use of biomarker testing to confirm cases of acute hepatitis. Testing strategies may involve simultaneous or sequential testing for biomarkers of recent infection, such as IgM antibodies for hepatitis A, B, C, and E. The testing should be provided free of charge to patients, and national SOPs should specify approved test kits with adequate sensitivity and specificity. Data management and analysis are critical components of the surveillance system. Only aggregated results will be shared, and personal identifiers will not be entered into electronic databases. Data analysis will focus on trends in case numbers, risk factors, and modes of transmission, which can inform public health interventions. The guidelines emphasize the protection of human subjects and the ethical considerations involved in surveillance activities. Patients will benefit from accurate diagnoses and counseling as part of routine healthcare. Informed consent will be obtained through an information sheet explaining the objectives of the surveillance and the use of anonymized data. Patients will have the option to opt out of participation without affecting their care. The WHO encourages countries to institutionalize sentinel surveillance systems for acute hepatitis and adapt the SOPs to their national context. The ultimate goal is to provide ministries of health with the technical guidance needed to monitor and respond to acute hepatitis cases, thereby contributing to the global effort to eliminate viral hepatitis as a public health threat.
